b: Recorded at the Octagon Unitarian Chapel in Norwich, the English composer and improviser welcomes in the season of Advent

Although we do not often think to question it, the church organ is a strange concept. Uniquely, it is tied to its location, more like a building than an instrument. While the organ triggers sound, the resonance of its building is what shapes it. The acoustics of every church or chapel are different, and every organ is therefore a unique instrument with a signature sound generated belonging to just one place. The place specificity of the church organ, and its responsiveness to conditions, was recently explored by Michael Cloud Duguay on his Kingdom Come, Kingdom Go album, recorded in Newfoundland churches. Similar concerns shape Laura Cannell’s new recording, Winter Rites. Cannell, Norfolk-based, recorded the six tracks on the album in the Octagon Unitarian Chapel in Norwich, an octagonally-shaped 18th-century brick building, just off Magdalen Street for those familiar with the Fine City.

The atmosphere on the album is tangibly chilly. Cannell is well-known for her extensive back catalogue using medieval-style instruments to generate deep, meditative drones that seem to emanate from the East Anglian landscape. Here, she sets out her intention to improvise a winter landscape, using the organ, a violin and a recorder. The acoustic profile of the space is communicated powerfully, with the music acting like sonar signals, mapping the open interior of the building. It seeps out into the damp Norwich lanes beyond, then along the River Wentsum and over the reed beds, first a mist then a fog, stretching out to the boundless horizons of the Broads. ‘Omnis Terra Floruit’, played on the organ, is a slow, layered construction, but full of unexpectedly dramatic moments, like the soundtrack to a wildlife documentary following the liminal gait of a hare crossing a frozen landscape.

The album is also inspired by Advent, an underrated season musically, much more interesting than Christmas, but almost entirely ignored. Cannell has taken Advent pieces by Hildegard of Bingen as the basis for her recorder improvisations on ‘O Splendidissima after Hildegard’ and ‘Ave Maria’. These pieces in particular sound like messages from a harder, sharper, clearer time. Hildegard’s communion with other dimensions is at the heart of these tracks – and the whole album, as Cannell seems to enter into a trance at times, seated at the console playing a single chord.

The doubled recorder lines dance over one another and reverberate around the octagonal walls. The album was recorded using microphones placed away from the source, on the balcony and on the opposite side of the chapel. There is a strong sense of sound crossing space in order to reach us. When the organ plays, it creates the immediate feeling that we have walked in through a church door and stopped to listen to somebody playing, unaware of our presence.

The closing piece, the 13-and-a-half minute ‘Omnis Ornamentis’ returns to the organ, bringing the pace down so gradually it is almost imperceptible, until we are suspended in a world of frost, visibility down to the hands stretched out in front of us. Winter is here, and we are surrounded by sound. Then, near the end of the piece, we can hear another layer of sound stretching over the register of the instrument, a faint human voice. It is Cannell, singing along as she plays.

Cannell’s work is remarkable, but what is more remarkable is her success. Who would have thought that the culture could embrace someone who is so unapologetically themselves and so focused on their musical path, with a complete absence of commercial compromise. She has hit a remarkable purple patch, with Winter Rites her tenth release since the start of 2025. This year, her various releases have made ten appearances in the UK Album Charts, and her impressively unpredictable credits include catwalk music for London, Milan and Paris Fashion weeks. Yet her music is a communication from another time, channelled through the fabric of the places around us, telling us we are not as significant as we imagine. It seems that we want to hear the message. Listen to this album with caution: you might find it is the only music you need.
